items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: That's why I say I really think that Trombauer was really such a great man with him. ... I'd say he almost fit in a category with Bix because everything they did, they did together

ctx.x: But Trombauer seemed to be the one who was most sympathetic to that kind of chord progression and things like that.

That's why I say I really think that Trombauer was really such a great man with him. I don't know. I think he's very neglected. Very neglected. I'd say he almost fit in a category with Bix because everything they did, they did together, you know? Yeah. Everything. I'm sure there was many ideas that Trombauer gave that helped Bix. Maybe we might say this. Maybe he didn't tell him what to play on, singing the blues or anything like that. But his inspiration, you know, would... Because I've played with musicians…
Oh, wonderful people. You just can't imagine. Wonderful people. And his wife, you know? His wife. You meet these guys, you know? And they didn't call her mama for that. She took care of everybody.

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: I believe it was a a very obscure record that they made by Joe Voyages bungalow dreams yeah they made Bix and Trombau

ctx.x: Before, I'm going to ask you to play a few things on the piano. Yeah. Because I think it shows the kind of thing you've been talking about with the piano and the cornet. But could you just relate the meeting with the Whiteman Orchestra at the St. Charles Theater? Yes. And I think it's an interesting story.

Well, I think it was probably one of the most exciting things that I can remember happening in my musical career. I don't know of any, I've had quite a few nice things happen, but this probably had to be one of the most exciting because, as I say, Bix was, well, it was a magic word at that time. And when we found out that Paul Whiteman was going to tour down this way and he was going to be at the St. Charles Theater, which is no longer here now, they tour it now. Why? This was something that everybody just looked…

come out there too. So we went back into the theater and when Mike Whiteman got finished playing Concerto O'NF by Gershwin, he put his baton on and he says, well, he says, all I can say is now, he says, I think I better turn it over to Bix and let him take over. He says, oh, they're going to tear this place down.

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: Trombaar took about three or four. Clarinet player would take about three or four, you know. Piano, banjo, they'd pass it around just like they, just like they do today, you know.

ctx.x: Were the numbers much longer than you hear on the records? Because usually records are limited to three minutes or something like that.

Oh, yeah, yes, oh, yes. I guess, I guess he stood up and maybe took about three or four, three or four solos one behind the other, you know. Trombaar took about three or four. Clarinet player would take about three or four, you know. Piano, banjo, they'd pass it around just like they, just like they do today, you know.
And that was longer than you hear on the records.
